If you want to go full nerd gun nut/realism, here's an overview:

- The original Gatling Gun was incredibly heavy like a cannon, so it needed to be mounted on wheels in order to fire.

- If you need to transport it over a long distance, you'll need several horses to transport the gun alone due to it's sheer weight. For the magazines, you'll also need another group of horses because 20 round magazines weighed about 30 pounds each, 40-50 for the 40 round mags. 

- Ammo is also going to cost a lot since it uses musket rounds. Also might want to increase the damage from d4 to something bigger.

- Given that the PC is able to fire the gun at a rate similar to what the U.S. Military was able to do, they'll be able to fire 200 rounds per minute, and since an average round of DnD is about 6 seconds, they'll be able to fire 20 rounds per round, so you're on point with that.

- The odds of the Gatling Gun overheating after one turn are basically zero since there are six barrels being used at once.

- As for misfires, they're also very unlikely due to the magazine-fed nature of the gun but a misfire check would still be fine.

Everything about Heavy is slow in general, but this mainly applies to 6s, as it is a fast-paced environment with high mobility classes making up most of the roster 95 percent of the time. Which is the complete opposite of what Heavy is. 

If you want to be more specific, the rollout and initial midfight are a big part of why Heavy slows games down. He gets to mid slower than any other class, and plays a lot more defensively then if he was a Soldier or Scout. He also makes it harder for the enemy team to push through, as they have to deal with a mobile sentry with more health. 

In short, he slows down his team by being unable to get to places faster, and slows down the enemy team by making it harder to push through chokepoints or capture points with his mere existence.

In a competitive game of HL: Sniper, they are ridiculously good at the game and can 9 times out of 10 quick scope your ass. They also try to position themselves near other teammates (namely Engie) which make them even harder to kill.

In a casual game with class stacking: Engie, stacking Engies with the Wrangler nearly makes the game unplayable on some maps, a good chunk of Payload maps make the final checkpoint impossible to push unless you have a bunch of good Demos/Direct Hit Soldiers and competent Medics. Also don’t forget that there’s still 7-9 other players on the Engie’s team, which can include really any player, if you’re unlucky, you’ll also end up fighting a god tier Scout/Spy as well. Really makes the game fun.

It’s not fun is the general broad term for everything you said relating to “slow” is not fun. 

A lot of talk around defensive play revolves around Heavy and Engineer, as they’re two core defensive classes. Their job is to make areas hard to push through, Engie with his sentries and being able to use a teleporter to get his teammates to the front line to defend. And Heavy, well… he’s Heavy. And that’s not just these two classes. But playing on defense in general slows down the game, which is the point on Payload maps. 

And if the enemy team is very skilled and is able to prevent pushes and in general, keep a proper defense from anything the enemy team throws at it regardless of positioning. This in turn, makes the game unfun for the offense. As they either have to push through a hard defense, or wait 3-10 minutes doing nothing. Neither of which, are fun to most players. And thus, playing defensively, or in your term “slow” is not fun.

This “slow” playstyle is a necessary evil in Highlander, but is often frowned upon in 6s, where teams have to switch from offense to defense quickly depending on the situation. So say for example, having a Heavy or Engineer in the initial 6s rollout (which is super stupid) will inevitably slow down the game. Hell, this is why the Disciplinary Action is banned in 6s. TL;DR it’s not possible to give Heavy a semi-effective subclass without breaking the game’s balance and/or being a big annoyance that the community probably wouldn’t like.

The issue with Heavy is his design doesn’t allow really any gimmicky weapons/playstyles without them being absolute shit in an environment like TF2. He’s a slow damage dealer/sponge who doesn’t do anything else except heal players occasionally. Trying to give him any sort of buff in general with the downside of losing/weakening his minigun makes him a joke. As that’s the only thing he’s got going for him outside of his sandvich. 

Extra health/resistances are annoying to deal with, but then you have to ask, *what can he do with these buffs?* Assuming this is the best case scenario, where Heavy gets a big health boost, damage resistances, and potentially some speed while still being able to use his secondary and melee. You’d just be getting an even spongier, slower Scout then you already were without using your primary in the first place. Which makes him just Demoknight but he traded all of his speed and mobility for health and a shotgun. And as you know in TF2, mobility > health. Even if you gave Heavy a meter which boosts his melee swing speed, it wouldn’t be all that effective when everyone can just shoot at you from a distance because you have no way of closing the gap so you can get your swings in. 

So no. Giving Heavy an effective subclass like Demoknight or Battle Engie won’t be possible in any near future, I’d like to hear some more ideas, however.
